# Fagus sylvatica
Fagus sylvatica

Species of deciduous tree

_**Fagus sylvatica**_, the **European beech** or **common beech**, is a large [deciduous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deciduous) tree in the [beech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagaceae) family with smooth silvery-grey bark, large leaf area, and a short trunk with low branches. [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-3) It is native to much of Europe, growing in humid climates.

The species is cultivated as an [ornamental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornamental_plant), and has been spread beyond its original range, including in North America. Numerous cultivars have been developed, including the showy copper beech, _Fagus sylvatica purpurea_. Although slightly toxic due to the [tannins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannin) and [alkaloids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaloid) they contain, the [nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nut_(fruit)) are consumed by animals and humans. The trees are used for timber, such as the making of furniture.

## Description
_Fagus sylvatica_ is a large [tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree), capable of reaching heights of up to 50 metres (160 feet) tall[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-4) and 3m (10ft) trunk diameter, though more typically 25–35m (82–115ft) tall and up to 1.5m (5ft) trunk diameter. A 10-year-old sapling will stand about 4m (13ft) tall. Undisturbed, the European beech has a lifespan of 300 years; one tree at the Valle Cervara site was more than 500 years old, the oldest known in the northern hemisphere. [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-5) In cultivated forest stands trees are normally harvested at 80–120 years of age.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-6) 30 years are needed to attain full maturity (as compared to 40 for [American beech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_grandifolia)). Like most trees, its form depends on the location; in forest areas, _F.sylvatica_ grows to over 30m (98ft), with branches being high up on the trunk. In open locations, it will become much shorter (typically 20m (66ft)) but more massive with a broader crown and stouter trunk.

The [leaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaves) are alternate, simple, and entire or with a slightly [crenate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crenate) margin, 5–10cm (2–3+7⁄8in) long and 3–7cm (1.2–2.8in) broad, with 6–7 veins on each side of the leaf (as opposed to 7–10 veins in _[F.orientalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_orientalis)_). When crenate, there is one point at each vein tip, never any points between the veins. The [buds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud) are long and slender, 15–30mm (5⁄8–1+1⁄8in) long and 2–3mm (3⁄32–1⁄8in) thick, but thicker, up to 4–5mm (1⁄8–1⁄4in), where the buds include flower buds.

The leaves of beech are often not [abscissed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abscission) (dropped) in the autumn and instead remain on the tree until the spring. This process is called [marcescence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcescence). This particularly occurs when trees are [saplings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapling) or when plants are clipped as a hedge (making beech hedges attractive screens, even in winter), but it also often continues to occur on the lower branches when the tree is mature.

The species is [monoecious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoecious). The male flowers are borne in small [catkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catkin),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-7) a hallmark of the [Fagales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagales) order. The female flowers produce beechnuts, small triangular [nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nut_(fruit)) 15–20mm (5⁄8–3⁄4in) long and 7–10mm (1⁄4–3⁄8in) wide at the base; there are two nuts in each cupule, maturing in the autumn 5–6 months after pollination. Flower and seed production is particularly abundant in years following a hot, sunny and dry summer, though rarely for two years in a row. Small quantities of seeds may be produced around 10 years of age, but not a heavy crop until the tree is at least 30 years old.

Spring leaf budding by the European beech is triggered by a combination of day length and temperature. Bud break each year is from the middle of April to the beginning of May, often with remarkable precision (within a few days). It is more precise in the north of its range than the south, and at 600m (2,000ft) than at [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level). [[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-8)

## Distribution and habitat
See also: [Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_and_Primeval_Beech_Forests_of_the_Carpathians_and_Other_Regions_of_Europe)

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Fagus_sylvatica_pliocenica_MHNT.PAL.VEG.2002.31.jpg/500px-Fagus_sylvatica_pliocenica_MHNT.PAL.VEG.2002.31.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fagus_sylvatica_pliocenica_MHNT.PAL.VEG.2002.31.jpg) _[Piacenzian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piacenzian)_ age fossil of _Fagus sylvatica pliocenica_

The European beech is the most abundant hardwood species in Austrian, German and Swiss forests. [[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-11) The native range extends from the north, in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden), [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark), [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany), [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland), [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland), [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria), western [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine), and [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania), through Europe to [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France), southern [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England), Spain (on the [Cantabrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantabrian_Mountains), [Iberian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Ib%C3%A9rico) and [Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Central) mountain ranges),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-12) [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-13) and east to northwest [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-POWO-2) where it exhibits an interspecific [cline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cline_(biology)) with the oriental beech ( _[Fagus orientalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_orientalis)_), which replaces it further east. In the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans), it shows some [hybridisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_(biology)) with oriental beech; these hybrid trees are named _[Fagus × taurica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_%C3%97_taurica)_ Popl. [ _Fagus moesiaca_ (Domin, Maly) Czecz.]. In the southern part of its range around the [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean) and [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-14) it grows only in mountain forests, at 600–1,800m (1,969–5,906ft) altitude.

Although often regarded as native in southern England, recent evidence suggests that _F. sylvatica_ did not arrive in England until about 4000 [BCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BCE), or 2,000 years subsequent to the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel) forming following the [ice ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period); it could have been an early introduction by [Stone Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Age) humans, who used the [nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nut_(fruit)) for food. [[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-15) The beech is classified as a native in the south of England and as a non-native in the north where it is often removed from 'native' woods. [[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-16) Localised pollen records have been recorded in the North of England from the [Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age) by Sir [Harry Godwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Godwin). It is often planted in Britain. Similarly, the nature of Norwegian beech populations is subject to debate. If native, they would represent the northern range of the species, although molecular genetic analyses imply that these populations represent intentional introduction from Denmark before and during the [Viking Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_Age). [[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-17) The beech in [Vestfold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestfold) and at Seim north of [Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen) in Norway is now spreading naturally and regarded as [native](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_plant). [[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-18)

The European beech tolerates a variety of soil types, but requires a humid atmosphere (with precipitation well distributed throughout the year) and well-drained soil. It prefers moderately fertile ground, calcified or lightly acidic, so it is found more often on the side of a hill than at the bottom of clayey basin. It tolerates rigorous winter cold, but is sensitive to spring frost. In Norway's oceanic climate planted trees grow well north to [Bodø Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bod%C3%B8_Municipality), and produce seedlings and can spread naturally in Trondheim. [[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-19) In Sweden, beech trees do not grow as far north as in Norway. [[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-20)

In the woodlands of southern Britain, beech is dominant over oak and elm south of a line from about north Suffolk across to Cardigan. Oak are the dominant forest trees north of this line. One of the most beautiful European beech forests called [Sonian Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonian_Forest) ( _Forêt de Soignes/Zoniënwoud_) is found in the southeast of Brussels, Belgium. Beech is a dominant tree species in France and constitutes about 10% of French forests. The largest [virgin forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_forest) made of beech trees are [Uholka-Shyrokyi Luh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uholka-Shyrokyi_Luh_primeval_beech_forest) (8,800 hectares or 22,000 acres) in Ukraine[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-Commarmot-2013-21) and Izvoarele Nerei (5,012ha or 12,380 acres in one forest body) in [Semenic-Cheile Carașului National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semenic-Cheile_Cara%C8%99ului_National_Park), [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania). These habitats are the home of Europe's largest predators, the brown bear, the grey wolf, and the lynx. [[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-24) Many trees are older than 350 years in Izvoarele Nerei[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-25) and even 500 years in Uholka-Shyrokyi Luh. [[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-Commarmot-2013-21)

## Cultivation
- copper beech or purple beech ( _Fagus sylvatica purpurea_)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-33) – a mutation of the European beech which was first noted in 1690 in the "Possenwald" forest near the town of [Sondershausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sondershausen) in Thuringia, Germany. It is assumed that about 99% of all copper beeches in the world are descendants of this copper beech. Its leaves are purple, often turning deep spinach green by mid-summer. In the United States Charles Sprague Sargent noted the earliest appearance in a nurseryman's catalogue in 1820, but in 1859 "the finest copper beech in America... more than fifty feet high" was noted in the grounds of Thomas Ash, Esq., [Throggs Neck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Throggs_Neck), New York;[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-34) it must have been more than forty years old at the time.
- fern-leaf beech ( _Fagus sylvatica_ Heterophylla Group) – leaves deeply serrated to thread-like
- [dwarf beech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwarf_beech) ( _Fagus sylvatica_ Tortuosa Group) – distinctive twisted trunk and branches
- [weeping beech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weeping_beech) ( _Fagus sylvatica_ Pendula Group) – branches pendulous
- Dawyck beech ( _Fagus sylvatica_ 'Dawyck') – fastigiate (columnar) growth – occurs in green, gold and purple forms; named after [Dawyck Botanic Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawyck_Botanic_Garden) in the Scottish Borders
- golden beech ( _Fagus sylvatica_ 'Zlatia') – leaves golden in spring

# _Fagus sylvatica_Play pronunciation
## Common Name(s):
### Previously known as:
It grows 50 to 60 feet tall and has dense, erect, oval to rounded crowns. Yellowish-green and reddish-brown flowers bloom from April to May.

This tree is a member of the _Fagaceae_ or beech family and is native to central and southern Europe to the Caucasus. It has become a popular ornamental shade tree.

The specific epithet, _sylvatica,_ is Latin and means "growing in the woods".

**Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems:** This tree has no serious insect pests or diseases.

## European Beech
The European beech is a stately addition to any large landscape and in time becomes an imposing shade tree. The simple foliage is dark green and somewhat shiny. The beech nuts it produces in the fall are attractive to wildlife. Autumn foliage is golden bronze; in winter the handsome gray bark is prominent.

The smooth gray bark is an attractive feature of the species.

The genus _Fagus_ includes 10-13 species of the beech tree, which are native to temperate regions of Asia, Europe and North America. Only _Fagus grandifolia_, the American beech, is native to the U.S. and Illinois. A single species, _Fagus sylvatica_ or the European beech, accounts for the vast majority of cultivars used in landscaping. The Chicago Botanic Garden's collections contain three species but more than two dozen varieties among its more than 100 beech trees.

Like their cousins the oaks, beech trees are long-lived and slow growing hardwood trees. The fruit produced annually is commonly called a beech nut and is beloved by wildlife. Beech trees are majestic shade trees at maturity. While tolerant of a wide range of soils, the genus prefers consistent and moderate moisture.
